To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the survival advantage of cesarean delivery is limited to extremely premature infants less than 25 weeks' gestation and that the absolute difference is small (2-4%).

the survival of very preterm infants delivered by cesareans has increased over time and that this survival advantage may be due to a reduction in the number of cesarean sections performed for maternal indications.
cesarean section is associated with improved survival of infants born at less than 26 0/7 weeks' gestation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the effects of cesarean delivery on neonatal mortality and morbidity.
the effects of the mode of birth on outcomes for very preterm and low-birthweight babies.
the effects of the cesarean section on the outcome of very low-birth-weight (less than 1500 grams) and very preterm (less than 28 weeks) infants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against the use of cesarean sections to improve outcomes in extremely immature infants.
the evidence for or against cesarean section in this population is not sufficient to justify a change in clinical practice.
there is no evidence to suggest that the outcomes of infants born less than 26 completed weeks' gestation are improved by cesarean delivery.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the data do not support a routine policy of cesarean section for all very preterm or very low-birth-weight infants.
the data are insufficient to justify routine cesarean section delivery for very preterm and low-birthweight births, but that the issue merits further study.
the evidence is insufficient to support a policy that cesarean section is preferable to vaginal delivery for these infants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the decision to perform a cesarean section for a very preterm infant is not a decision to be taken lightly.
the decision to deliver a very preterm or very low-birth weight infant by cesarean should be made on a case-by-case basis.
we should not assume that all cesareans are good and all vaginal deliveries are bad.
